responseSet.title: Martha Harris (1920-1986)
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Martha Harris (1920-1986)

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin  

Mattie Harris died last November at her home in Oxford. She had been ill since her tragic accident two and a half years earlier. Sad as this final period of her life had been, the loss which her death represented was a great one for her family and friends.

The early years of her life were spent on a Scottish farm, and her love of Scotland remained intense throughout her life. The heather colours so often seen on her person and in her home were indications of her fond re-creation of this beloved landscape. She was the eldest of four children, and enjoyed a lot of childhood pleasures with her two sisters and younger brother. For those who came to know her later, her beautiful soft breathy Scottish voice was one of her most treasured attributes. Her words tumbled over each other at times, always conveying the impression of Mattie's eager vitality. There was so much to say and understand, and most things were worth noticing and thinking about.

When she was eight years old, her family moved South and she spent those later years of childhood in Sussex, as part of a transplanted Scottish dairy-farming community. She enjoyed her school years hugely and threw herself into academic and sporting activities, dramatic productions, and an individualist's battling relationship with her school. She did very well at school and was determined to have a university education, so she taught herself the necessary Latin in a few months to fulfil university entrance requirements. She studied English Literature at London University, and her knowledge and appreciation of literature proved a continuously creative spring in her later career as a child psychotherapist and psychoanalyst. Indeed, she felt that her literary training had prepared her well for such work, and although she later acquired a psychology degree, the literary background was what she most valued.

She spent some years as a teacher, and then in 1950 came to the Tavistock Clinic, then in its old building in Beaumont Street, to train as a child psychotherapist in the newly established training programme organized by Esther Bick and John Bowlby. She was one of the second group of students to train, and her peers included Dina Rosenbluth and Frances Tustin.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Analysis of a Well-Endowed Boy from an Emotionally Impoverished Environment

Frances Salo

Frances Salo

9 Somali Road
London NW2

Frances Salo  

Three-and-a-half-year-old Robin had never had a night's undisturbed sleep. In his battles with his mother he was so dominating that she described him as “like a giant”. But the picture he presented in his first diagnostic interview was such that the diagnosticians considered whether he might be dull or possibly deaf. There was a pervasive inhibition and in particular a restriction in pleasurable play, although once or twice his use of language was amusing, as when he talked of soldiers as “shooter-pushers”.

One year after referral Robin was a confident and extremely competent child, whose ability to captivate was evident. His play had matured and it was striking how well his activities were chosen for their expressive value. He was regarded as one of the brightest children in his nursery class. The hints of his verbal charm which peeped through at the assessment flowered in the analysis and the words would come tumbling out as we walked upstairs. No longer a fearful child, he would scale up and down the lockers in our room with a natural agility. He was as passionate in his love relationships after treatment as he had been in fighting his parents before treatment. I hope to show in this paper how the transformation took place.

At the beginning of treatment we were dubious of the outcome. We questioned the parents' ability to sustain the treatment. Mrs C. had an extended period of mother guidance in another clinic and had found this unhelpful. Then the C.s lived a considerable distance from the Centre, which meant that Robin's younger toddler brother would spend up to three hours of his day travelling and in our waiting room. But the parents did want help for Robin even if it was at times close to a wish for Robin to be “made good”.

A number of factors will have contributed to the improvement seen in Robin. Firstly, there was his intelligence which, in the course of the diagnostic assessment, was found to be of at least good average or higher and, in particular, his facility with language. His nursery class seems to have provided him with an appropriately stimulating environment and to be another place where his talents were recognized. Obviously there were also maturational factors, from which Robin was increasingly able to profit as treatment freed certain areas. But I do not think that he could have profited fully from them had it not been for treatment, and the work with his parents, and I will give a separate account of these.

[[RunningHead]]

Lydia A.H. Smith; To Understand and to Help: The Life and works of Susan Isaacs (1885-1948). Published by Associated University Presses, 1985. Hardback £27.95.

Rolene Szur

Rolene Szur

Rolene Szur  

This study of Susan Isaacs and her work introduces the reader to a personality who emerges with great intellectual strength and independence as well as insight and humanity. The qualities are conveyed very largely through the presentation of her work, and more specifically her work in the field of education. In turn this is related to a period of intense debate on and interest in issues of childhood development and approaches to education. The author, who is Professor of Education at Simmons College Boston, has a special interest in English sources of informal education (1976). This it seems increasingly drew her towards more detailed explorations of Susan Isaac's work and research into teaching methods that might be based on a “thorough understanding of the value of play and direct experience”.

The biographical details of Mrs. Isaacs' early life are summarized in a few pages, from which we learn that she was born Susan Fairhurst in 1885, the ninth child of a Methodist lay preacher, who was also a journalist, and his wife in Bromley Cross, near Bolton, Lancashire. Before she was eight months old, a brother just a little older than herself, died. When she was three, another and much-loved older brother left to join the merchant navy. She was only four years old when her mother became seriously ill and died two years later.

Strictness and conformity appear to have dominated in the household and in her disappointing experiences at school. However her enthusiasm for learning remained undimmed, prompted readings in philosophy, a conversion to agnosticism and a consequent two-year estrangement from her father, who therefore withdrew her from school (not yet aged 15). Formal education was not resumed again until the age of twenty-two, with her father's permission, at Manchester University. Here she trained initially as a teacher with a special interest in primary schools, but then moved on to take a first class honours degree in philosophy. This was followed by a change of direction towards biology, psychology, and research into psychology along biological lines. When she later became interested in psychoanalysis she entered into analysis with J.C. Flugel and became a member of the British Psychoanalytic Society in 1923. Interest in Mrs. Klein's work with very young children prompted her to a second analysis with Joan Rivière, and Susan Isaacs referred to her own “deep sense of the fundamental psychological research which the analytic technique with very young children makes possible” (p. 130).

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Jean Liedloff: The Continuum Concept. Published by Penguin Books Ltd., 1986. Paperback, £3.50.

Frances Salo

Frances Salo

Frances Salo  

First published twelve years ago, this book was reissued in a revised version by Penguin Books last year and many readers may by now be familiar with it, even if only by hearsay. Jean Liedloff, from 212 years spent living with the Yequana tribe, in South America, a non-aggressive tribe of “Stone Age” Indians, attempts to extrapolate from what she observed there a universal philosophy of life with far-reaching implications for bringing up children, and to apply it to present-day Western society.

I shall first try to convey something of what Ms Liedloff means by the continuum concept. For some two million years humankind functioned in harmony with nature with an instinctive sense of the Tightness of things, a Tightness which was handed down over time, thus forming a continuum. She therefore sees Western culture as a deviant aberration over a relatively short period of time so that we are still born with this knowledge within ourselves and we would be able to return to this.

She spells out some of what follows from this sense of Tightness. From birth onwards a baby needs (total) skin contact, and is in torment if she does not have this twenty-four hours a day; this includes bathing with her mother and sleeping with the parents even during lovemaking. She is thus happily in the midst of constant activity without artificially being the centre of attention. This period of in-arms experience would usually last for about 6-8 months, by which time the infant would be ready to begin moving away from her mother. Her mother would be there in the background if the infant needed her but she would provide the minimum of supervision, trusting the infant's judgement not to hurt herself, say, on the numerous machetes which are lying around. Children are seen as inherently social, inherently wanting to comply with society's expectation of them and are allowed to make many of their own decisions to a staggering degree from toddlerhood onwards. Ms Liedloff's vision of perfect harmony depicts a nuclear family with stereotypical sex-typing of roles, the boys with the men, the girls helping the women with the housework and so on.

[[RunningHead]]

Frances Tustin: Autistic Barriers in Neurotic Patients. Published by Karnac Books & Yale University Press, 1986. Paperback, £9.95.

Sheila Spensley

Sheila Spensley

Sheila Spensley  

Since the discovery of infantile autism by Kanner, a number of distinguished psychoanalysts have made steady advances in understanding this strangely aberrant condition. Margaret Mahler brought autism within the orbit of normal infant development while Meltzer and his co-workers have offered psychodynamic models. Now Frances Tustin brings a new dimension to our understanding by linking autism and its phenomena to our ontological development and inheritance.

In this, her third book she develops further her view, first adumbrated in Autistic States (1981) that disturbances at an autistic level are yet to be found at the core of many common adult psychopathological disorders. Her formulations are original and far-reaching and the integration of her thinking into Kleinian theory may have implications for clinical practice and even for some fundamental conceptions about infant development itself. These questions are developed by Grotstein in his forward to the Yale University Press edition. It is unfortunate that this was not available for Karnac's publication. It is a serious loss, for Grotstein addresses clinical and theoretical implications which help the reader to orient Tustin's highly original contribution within the mainstream of the development of psychoanalytic thinking.

Frances Tustin's work has been translated into a number of languages and, in many respects, receives more active attention in Europe than in England where the field of autism and mental retardation has been dominated by behavioural and cognitive psychology. That her discoveries reach far beyond the confines of that area expediently termed “mental handicap” is clear; paradoxically, there is danger of their relevance being lost to the very field in which the discoveries were made. Mrs. Tustin has devoted many years to the treatment of that group of mentally handicapped children whom Leo Kanner first identified and differentiated from the organically impaired in 1943. These children seem to have suffered a severe psychogenic impairment, but even within this group she is careful not to imply that psychotherapy is always appropriate and stresses the importance of very early treatment before the very powerful autistic protectors become impregnable.

[[RunningHead]]

Working with other Professionals in an In-Patient Setting

Deborah Bandler

Deborah Bandler

14 Chalcot Gardens
London NW3 4YB

Deborah Bandler  

When a number of professionals are involved in treating the same family it becomes necessary to think about how to work together. In this paper I would like to focus on ways of working together used at the Cassel Hospital, in the in-patient Families Unit. Although the structures we use may not be applicable or appropriate to other settings, the thinking and the underlying principles hopefully will be.

An in-depth picture of the work of the Families Unit can be found in The Family as In-patient (R. Kennedy, A. Heymans, L. Tischler, eds, 1987). For purposes of this paper, I will begin by giving a brief outline of the treatment, the setting and the staff involved in the work. Some further details will follow later in the paper.

The Families Unit is one for up to 8 families, with 26 beds available. Although any family member may be the referred “patient”, die main concern most often centres on the parent/s. Families are referred when family functioning has broken down. Examples are: cases of puerperal breakdown; Severely neurotic or borderline disturbance in the parent/s which makes looking after the children impossible; children in care, often because of physical or sexual abuse, where the main aim is to reunite them with their parents. The hospital functions as a therapeutic community, with emphasis for families on looking after their children (there are also 2 units for single adults). Professionals involved with each family include: therapist/s for the parents, who are usually seen individually; child therapist/s treating the children; a nurse for the family whose aim is to facilitate the family's capacity to carry out the everyday tasks of functioning. There is also a Day Unit for the children, staffed by a teacher and nurses. These are main workers, but the family will also come into contact with other staff (nurses, social worker, consultants, etc.). The setting is a large, rambling, but somehow “homely” building.

It is of course an advantage to have the professionals working with a family all in the same building: it is therefore theoretically possible to talk to one another without too much difficulty. Yet I do not think anyone would assume that this makes the working together, necessarily proceed any more smoothly. For it is inevitable that working with troubled families causes considerable strain for those involved in helping them.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Internal Conflict and Growth in a Child Preparing to Start School

Denis Flynn

Denis Flynn

57 Lock Road
Ham, Richmond
Surrey

Denis Flynn  

The transition from home to school is one of the most important changes in the life of a developing child. Separation problems, which have their roots in the child's earliest experiences, generally become more evident at this time. Also the child's own route through early stages of development and individuation may receive a jolt, when he or she is faced with the demands of a more social situation, with its increased need for restraint and uniformity, and its new opportunities to make relationships with children and adults, especially teachers.

I shall outline a case-study about a girl of three and a half years called Georgina, who came for three times weekly psychotherapy for one and a half years before starting school, when she reduced to once weekly. I shall describe her internal conflicts as her anxieties about going to school increased, and the parallel between the separation from home and parents and her experience of separation in the transference relationship with the psychotherapist. I aim to show that her achievement in working through intense infantile conflicts was of central impotance to her making a successful social change, the transition from home to life at school.

Georgina was referred to a child guidance clinic at the age of three and a half. The whole family were offered an initial appointment but father did not come because of pressure of work. Georgina was reportedly progressing well in most areas, but her mother, insistent that there was a hold up in her development was intensely upset about Georgina's behaviour: her repeated aggression towards her nine months old brother, Jason, and her wetting and soiling. (Georgina had in fact been toilet-trained before the age of two.) She found Georgina to be alternately clinging, then distant and unmanageable. She was dismayed that Georgina was hated by children in the vicinity and at her playgroup because of her attacks on them. She dated the beginning of the difficulties from the time Georgina went to nursery, aged two and a half. These difficulties increased after Jason's birth and ever since then there had been a strained relationship with her.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Searching for a Lost One: The Plight of the Family of the Autistic Child

Maurice Whelan and Willis Hudson

Willis Hudson

43 Cricklewood Lane
London NW2

48 Camberley Avenue
London SW20

Willis Hudson  

“Come away, Oh human child!

To the waters and the wild

With a faery, hand in hand,

For the world's more full of weeping than you

can understand.”

“The Stolen Child”, W.B. Yeats

In this poem the fairies beckon the child and entice him to leave a world that is “full of troubles and is anxious in its sleep”. They offer a leafy island with “pools among the rushes that scarce could bathe a star”, where ferns “drop their tears over the young streams”. Fairies however are not always offering an eternal youthful Peter Pan world. In Ireland the “Sidhe” is a name given to a fairy who is usually construed as being far from benign. Children whose mental development has been severely impaired or retarded can be spoken of as if this “Sidhe” had taken their souls away. This idea is not unique to Irish myth. In “Totem and Taboo” Freud refers to a similar phenomenon where the soul is taken and replaced by another. Scottish myth tells of the fairy who can touch you and leave you distant and dissociated. Hence the word “fay”. Being presented with an autistic child is a baffling and puzzling experience. Enter the poet who through his medium can convey an experience which is difficult to explain and which defies prosaic reasoning.

Autistic children are very distant and it is almost impossible to know what is going on in their minds. We can sometimes get an approximation by our own strange experiences. Perhaps the hallucinations of our dreams give us some insight into the reality of the mind of such a child. A dreamer dreams that he is travelling from London to Edinburgh, however in his dream he is moving from west to east. The world has been turned sideways. The equator has become the North and the South Poles. The arctic and antarctic now face direct sunlight. Images of this kind perhaps convey to us some of the world of the autistic child. Where does one start? What are one's reference points? In what direction is one travelling? Has the autistic child gone away to the world of fairies, elves and goblins?

[[RunningHead]]

Dangerous Building Keep Out: An Account of a Psychotic Girl's Psychotherapy

Adrian Sutton

Adrian Sutton

Manchester, M14 5NP

Adrian Sutton  

Introduction

This paper is principally intended as an account of the main events in a psychotic girl's psychotherapy. I saw her twice-weekly for eighteen months starting from the age of ten and a half years and finishing a few days after her twelfth birthday, when she reached the upper age limit of the hospital and had to leave. From the material I will describe certain ‘rules' which governed the girl's experience of life. The nature of these sometimes led her to seek refuge by withdrawing from the outside world; at other times they left her too unsafe to be able to learn or have the freedom to develop or change her ideas. These ‘rules' were manifested in her use of various items such as her body and its sensations, sticks, paper models and also in her variable ability to feel safe in having any form of relationship with me. The ‘rules' changed and what I wish to present here are some of the ways these changes showed themselves. The most comprehensive and helpful material from the literature in formulating this account were those of Meltzer et al (1975) and Tustin (1981).

A second issue, which I address more briefly is the contribution psychotherapy can make where there have been problems of diagnosis. In a description of the institution in which the child presented here was being treated, G. Stroh (1974) give five diagnostic categories for the children admitted to the hospital. These are: childhood autism, organic with autistic features, schizophrenia, traumatic psychosis, ESN psychosis. His use of the first three categories is identical with the description in “The International Classification of Diseases (1978)”, but he defines the latter two within his own frame of reference. They share with the other groups severe pervasive developmental disturbance, bizarre symptomatology and grossly impaired relationships but are differentiated on the basis of history and progress in treatment. The characteristics of the traumatic psychosis group is that their disturbance is associated with or caused by “early experiences of violence which the child had either experienced himself or has witnessed in his intimate environment, or both” (p. 179). Stroh's fifth group of ESN psychosis are differentiated by the “relative non-descriptiveness” since they “emerged, paradoxically, by not emerging at all” (p. 181). They display neither the violence of the traumatic groups nor the extreme behaviours of autistic or schizophrenic children. Stroh gives further details of both types of child and also of their families. Using the multiaxial system of the International Classification of Diseases (1978), Rutter (1985, p. 558) describes two subgroups of children with pervasive developmental disturbance similar to Stroh's fourth and fifth groups.

Neville Symington: The Analytic Experience: Lectures from the Tavistock. Published by Free Association Books, 1986. Hardback, £22.50 Paperback, £8.95.

Isca Wittenberg

Isca Wittenberg

Isca Wittenberg  

This is an unusual and exciting book in many ways. One of the ways in which it is unusual is that it combines the presentation of Freudian and post-Freudian theories and concepts with a demonstration of how and to what extent these have been useful to the author in the practice of psychoanalysis. It is exciting in that Neville Symington succeeds, to an extent which no other author I've come across does, in leading the reader through his musing and clinical illustrations to glimpse something of the essential flavour of the analytic process and the atmosphere within the consulting room. He comes from many angles at his central task of trying to convey what psychoanalysis is, concerning himself with what is truth, insight, and meaning, within the psychoanalytic setting. He shows us how analyst and patient are struggling with their attempts and resistances to arrive at understanding the truth about what is going on between them and how this leads to a deep understanding of the patient's personality. The book can thus serve as a helpful introduction to psychoanalysis for the general reader: it can equally help professionals in making up their mind whether to embark on a personal analysis or recommend it to others.

The book is of equal, if not greater, importance for therapists, for it examines how the psychoanalytic work affects the analyst as well as the patient. The honesty with which the analyst's mind at work in situations of stress is revealed reminded me of Patrick Casement's Learning From the Patient, another remarkably courageous book, published a year before the one under review here. It is indeed reassuring to know that psychoanalysis has reached a degree of maturity which allows some analysts to share their thinking about patients' material and their learning on the basis of self-examination and clinical mistakes.

Psychotherapeutic Interventions in Cases of Impaired Mother/Infant Relationships

Stella Acquarone

Stella Acquarone

27 Frognal
London NW3 6AR

Stella Acquarone  

This paper will describe different psychotherapeutic interventions in cases of impaired mother/infant relationships. The idea arose from the following:

There is a group of children who, from birth, are reported to have difficulty thriving, bonding, coping with anxiety or tolerating frustrations. The mother's attitude often contributes to this problem. The result is emotional disturbance, expressed as screaming continuously for no apparent reason, breath-holding, feeding difficulties, vomiting where no cause can be found, etc.

There is a common pattern in children referred for psychotherapy, special education, fostering, institutionalisation or non-accidental injury. From a very early stage of their development, these children have shown symptoms that have been confirmed by the professionals working with them. These symptoms could vary from sleeping difficulties, withdrawal, hyperactivity, proneness to accidents, etc.

The main objectives are: to explore a variety of impaired mother/infant relationships in the hope that this will contribute to the basis for further exploration of technical and theoretical issues in this area; and to offer a framework for intervention at the earliest possible stage.

Background to This Work

Drs Johnson, Dowling and Wesner mounted a maternal/infant programme at the Milwaukee Health Centre where the distressed infant was encouraged to take the lead and the mother was asked to follow its behaviour as unobtrusively as possible, for an hour a week. Johnson et al used the mother as therapist and mother/baby interaction was supervised with the aid of a video. The psychotherapist was directed to sensory-motor patterns of response. Unfortunately the investigators did not believe that psychic awareness could be functioning at this age, so subtle symbolic interactions were not examined. Other workers have most frequently treated the distressed infant by working with the mother. Contributions in this area include the work of Brazelton et al (1971) and Fraiberg et al (1967). [[RunningHead]]

Incest in Psychic Reality

Caroline Gluckman

Caroline Gluckman

2 Alma Terrace
Allen Street
London, W8 6QY

Caroline Gluckman  

Susan, aged nearly sixteen, was the first of a recent burst of referrals of sexually abused children to the clinic where I work. This dramatic increase is, I believe, a typical experience in Child Guidance Clinics throughout the country and provides some food for thought. Over a period of some eighteen months I found myself engaged in therapies of different durations with six such children, all girls, four of whom had experienced an incestuous sexual relationship with their natural father within a family situation.

Susan, as the eldest and most ready to link her difficulties openly to the incestuous relationship to her father, which had taken place in latency, provided an interesting but brief insight into the problem. She withdrew from therapy after only four months, maintaining that she was better. My sense of the unfinished nature of the work with Susan, together with my awareness of the increasing number of such referrals raised the question of how to respond to a growing problem which might require particular understanding. My interest was less in the reasons for this sudden increase, about which I could speculate, than with what it could mean to a child and some of its likely consequences. I felt the need to look beyond what Freud (1913) called our instinctive “horror of incest”, and our natural revulsion on hearing accounts of some of the sexual exploits small children are subjected to by adults in their environment, to try and come to some clearer picture of its significance in terms of a child's development. In particular, I was concerned with its meaning in terms of psychic reality and the kind of defence mechanisms which might come into play.

In presenting some ideas from the available literature together with reflections based on my own experience, I have used clinical material from Susan in some detail as well as extracts from the therapy of a much younger child who recently started weekly sessions with me, six-year-old Kali. The focus here most directly concerns situations of father/daughter incest but has, I think, a wider relevance.

[[RunningHead]]

Failure of the Holding Relationship: Some Effects of Physical Rejection on the Child's Attachment and on His Inner Experience

Juliet Hopkins

Juliet Hopkins

Tavistock Clinic
120 Belsize Lane
London, NW3

Juliet Hopkins  

Introduction

Bowlby's immense contribution to our awareness of the importance of holding in the early mother-child relationship was acknowledged by Winnicott in his last public lecture (1970). “John Bowlby has done more than one man's share of drawing the world's attention to the sacredness of the early holding situation and the extreme difficulties that belong to the work of those that try to mend it.”

In this paper I shall participate in Bowlby's work of drawing attention to the early holding situation, in order to consider some implications for the child psychotherapist in trying both to understand and to mend it.

Winnicott's term, “the holding situation”, was used by him to cover many aspects of the early mother-child relationship besides the actual physical holding of the baby. But here I intend to restrict myself to that aspect alone: that is, to the mother's provision of physical holding and body contact for her young child. I intend to illustrate its significance by reference to the response of children whose mothers, though present, are physically rejecting of their infants. I shall bring together contributions from attachment research and clinical work, and finally consider some implications for psychotherapy.

The role of holding in the early mother-child relationship was never developed as a theme by Freud. Winnicott pointed out that Freud himself had enjoyed good enough mothering to be able to take many aspects of its reliability for granted and to provide them for his patients in the secure and comfortable setting of his consulting room. Winnicott set out to remedy Freud's omission of the theme of holding; he developed original ideas about the role of holding in the mother-infant relationship and its parallels in the analytic situation. In 1952 he wrote that “the earliest anxiety is related to being insecurely held”, and followed this with the statement that the physical holding of the infant is a form of loving (1960a). “It is perhaps the only way in which a mother can show the infant her love.” In 1963 he described how the analyst symbolically holds the patient and how “this often takes the form of conveying in words at the appropriate moment something that shows that the analyst knows and understands the deepest anxiety that is being experienced or that is waiting to be experienced”. Clearly this implies that the function of holding, in addition to conveying love, is to relieve anxiety. It follows that a child who is not adequately held must feel both unloved and anxious.

[[RunningHead]]

Saying “No” to Psychotherapy: Consultation and Assessment in a Case of Sexual Abuse

Susan Dyke

Susan Dyke

32 Swaffield Road
London SW18 3AQ

Susan Dyke  

This is an account of my involvement in the case of two sisters, Janet (5) and Emma (3), who were referred in an atmosphere of crisis to the child guidance clinic where I work. Janet had been raped by a 16-year-old boy and both their parents had also been arrested in separate charges of child sexual abuse (CSA). There were urgent and repeated requests from the social worker involved for psychiatric help for the children. Known normally for being relatively sensible and contained in her work, she was telephoning the clinic with increasing urgency demanding immediate intervention.

The experiences of the following four months were extremely instructive ones, and in this paper I wish to share them and to reflect on the pressures to take into psychotherapy children whose primary needs for the time being lie elsewhere, especially in cases of CSA. Psychotherapists all over the country must be, as I am, frequently receiving requests to offer treatment to the wave of CSA referrals' emerging from recent publicity, and it seems highly important to give some thought as to both whether and when psychotherapy is the response these children need in the aftermath of disclosure.

I also hope to show how indirect consultative help can be of greater use at a time of crisis and upheaval, and in the process, to isolate some of the emotional factors particular to such children and their caretakers. I will not be discussing the assessment itself in detail, as this would raise other issues beyond the scope of this paper that need serious consideration in their own right.

The Background

It should be stressed that much of the following material only emerged piecemeal, much only becoming clear at a very late stage of the consultation. Such was the pressure on the social worker and foster mother that one of the first casualties was the capacity to convey clear and coherent information to us.

As is so often the case with CSA, Janet and Emma's story combined a long-term background of emotional difficulty and an immediate trauma. There had long been concern about the general standard of care given the children by their parents, which increased as their needs became more diverse and after a third child was born (Tommy, the youngest, was 10 months at the time of referral). The social workers' reports reveal that the children were unwashed and smelly most of the time, had irregular meals and were often ignored by their parents who only responded when it suited them. The family had been long known to the Social Services (SSD).

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

On Aesthetic Reciprocity

Donald Meltzer

Donald Meltzer

Oxford

Donald Meltzer  

We know from ethology the powerful effect of imprinting in establishing a bond at a primitive level, the level of adhesive types of identification, of conditioned reflexes and of automatic obedience (or disobedience?). We want to trace and explore the comparable phenomena at the level of mentality — of emotion, symbol formation, thought and judgment. There is indisputable evidence from the analytic therapy of psychotic children that the bonding at the imprinting level can be overridden by a failure of emotional bonding. Where this occurs we have been overly ready, as psychiatrists, to ascribe this deficit to extrinsic factors: foetal distress, immaturity, prolonged labour, etc. Almost always one can find some such extrinsic factor on which to hang a causal explanation. But the therapeutic process with such children suggests a far more intrinsic problem that requires our understanding. It has no explanatory power and must remain somewhat conjectural, but it is powerfully evocative. We want to suggest that these children, in one way or another, have been overwhelmed by the aesthetic impact of the outside world and the prime object that represents it both concretely and symbolically: the mother, her breasts and nipples, and her eyes and mind.

If we are to pursue this idea seriously, it is necessary likewise to confront the even more difficult question: why are not all babies so overwhelmed? Or are they bowled over but saved, in the nick of time, as it were, by something? I am going to describe a child who emerged crushed physically as well as mentally: Claudia, now eight years old. The consortium of extrinsic factors contributory to her crushing and the therapeutic equipment, including analysis, that has contributed to her rejuvenation, are equally impressive. But the content of the analysis suggests a very surprising formulation of instrinsic factors, products of her mentality. It suggests that Claudia was not saved from being crushed by the aesthetic impact of her beautiful mother because she experienced her mother seeing her as “an ugly little clown”. Furthermore the material of the analysis suggests that she understood this to be a fact, that she was an ugly little clown, by virtue of the method by which she had been made, an ugly method. This latter explanation appears to have been the fruit of Claudia's later researches and thoughts about her parents and their relationship.

[[RunningHead]]

Explorations with Families

Beta Copley

Beta Copley

25 Pilgrims Lane
London NW3 1SX

Beta Copley  

In this paper I attempt to look at the nature and purpose of explorations with families and discuss possible indications for such work. I then turn to think about the relationship of the child psychotherapist in particular to work with families.

Explorations with families can take different forms and have varied outcomes. An initial contact with a family can range from a short consultation to a more dynamic brief intervention. It may or may not be an introduction to further work, either with the family as a whole, or with individual members. The term “exploration” seems preferable to that of “assessment” because it has a more dynamic connotation, allowing for the possibility of something being accomplished within such a process itself. “Exploration” also lends itself more readily to the idea of a two-way process. Feelings within a family about the nature of the service and the institution offering it may need to be thought about openly; it should not be solely a matter of an assessment of a potentially “suitable case for treatment” being made by the institution. “Assessment” can carry both passive and persecutory connotations, with implications of being assessed “for” something — and possibly found wanting.

The Field Family: A Family Consultation

Mr. and Mrs. Field requested a private consultation for themselves and their eighteen-year-old son, Ken; they said they were concerned about him in general, but in particular sought help following his two recent convictions for travelling without a rail ticket. (Although a private consultation the issues discussed here are also relevant to work in a clinic.) As the parents were asking for help about what they saw as Ken's problem, a family intervention with the potential of bringing these factors together seemed appropriate. Having established that Ken was the only child living at home, and willing to be seen with his parents, I agreed to see them as they suggested, offering a few exploratory sessions in which we could consider together whether more help, and of what kind, was needed.

[[RunningHead]]

Three Years of Infant Observation with Mrs. Bick

Jeanne Magagna

Jeanne Magagna

Pond Street
London, NW3

Jeanne Magagna  

Introduction

Some years ago Mrs. Harris* contacted me to lead an infant observation seminar for social workers. Although I had observed one infant before, I felt inadequately equipped for the task and so I asked Mrs. Bick for supervision of my observation of a young baby. For those of you who do not know of Mrs. Bick, she was an adult and child psychoanalyst, born in Poland. Some fifty years ago she did a Phd. on infant development with Charlotte Bühler in Vienna. In order to study some twins, she was required to use a stop-watch to count the number of social reponses the twins made towards each other. At this time she decided that to understand the development of the human personality, without being dictated to by all the current theories of personality development, she should study the ordinary life of a baby in his family environment. In 1948, when she began teaching at the Tavistock Clinic, at the request of Dr. John Bowlby, she initiated the training method of having psychotherapy trainees visit a family and observe the development of an infant from birth to two years.

I began the observations of the infant and his family when Mrs. Bick was 79. This was her last formal teaching experience. Mrs. Bick had written three articles on the importance of-infant observation and she was intensely interested in pursuing the contribution of infant observation to psychoanalytic work. She was also very well-known by former students as having extremely exacting standards for the observations. Mrs. Bick was eager to have every little detail of the observation, in order that she could experience with Proustian clarity the relationship between the baby and his family. I was aware that she was facing the end of her life as the baby began his. It seemed to me that her own in-touchness with the anxieties of dying enabled her to bring alive with utmost sensitivity the baby's fears of dissolution. Mrs. Bick had such an enthusiasm for infant observation that somehow my individual supervision with her became a seminar of 6-13 child psychotherapists who were doing a second infant observation. One year of observing became extended to three years of weekly observations which I presented to the seminar.

Lynda Miller

Lynda Miller  

It is ironic and perhaps also rather sad that a retrospective reading through of my mother and infant observations, which comprised an essential part of my pre-clinical training, led me to formulate the title of this paper. The irony and sadness lie, I think, in the contrast between this mother's highly idealized conscious ideas about breast-feeding, and the less conscious and unconscious processes by which the breast seemed to become a devalued and at times contemptible object for her baby.

I observed this mother, Jenny, with her baby, Anna, on a weekly basis over a period of two years, and subsequently on infrequent occasions. At the time of Anna's birth, Jenny and her boyfriend Michael, both of whom are Australian, were living in a “commune” in a large semi-derelict house with a group of friends. Inside, the room shared by the couple was brightly painted and well cared for, and the parents-to-be were adamant that their first child would be born in their home with as little medical intervention as possible.

At my first meeting with Jenny and Michael they emphasized to me their particular views on child-rearing, and they both seemed to adhere quite rigidly to an “alternative” ideology by which certain ideas and practices were deemed good as opposed to others which were seen as extremely bad. To give some of the most relevant examples: Jenny felt that a hospital birth would inevitably produce a traumatized and damaged baby, and she warned me that observations might be impeded by the fact that she intended to carry the baby next to her body all the time. She also made frequent references to the “vegan” diet which she followed, consisting of a very limited range of health foods which she felt were “pure” as opposed to the “contaminated” food eaten by most people in our culture; in particular, any animal product.

In accord with the parents' wishes, Anna was born at home amongst a circle of close friends. Jenny gave birth in a supported squatting position, and after seven hours of labour Anna was delivered into a bath of warm water and in Jenny's words “lay there smiling, looking all around”. Jenny reported triumphantly that no drugs at all had been needed, and that the fight she had anticipated having with her doctor if he tried to make her take a drug to expel the placenta had not even been necessary, as it had come away naturally.

Phyllis Grosskurth: Melanie Klein. Published by Hodder & Stoughton, 1986 Hardback £19.95, Paperback £11.95.

Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows  

Grosskurth's major biography of Klein is a fascinating and very readable account of this impressive woman's life. It is that impressiveness that is, perhaps, the strongest image one is left with on reading this book from which Klein emerges as totally committed to her work and resolute and uncompromising in endeavouring to secure a future for her ideas.

For me, the most interesting section is that concerned with the period around the time of the Controversial Discussions. By then Klein had formulated some of her most distinctive and original ideas and gained sufficient of a following for it to be possible to speak of a Kleinian group within the British Society. The arrival of the Freuds and of the Viennese analysts at the time of the Second World War led to major political wrangles in which the control of training — e.g. the allocation of candidates to particular analysts — emerged as a central issue, besides the scientific disagreements. Grosskurth's account illuminates the character of numerous of the participants in these struggles, particularly of Glover, Jones and Klein's daughter Melitta. These dissensions were, one sees, so severe that there was at times a real danger of the Society splitting, until the present ‘A’ and ‘B’ group arrangement was settled upon. The knowledge gained of this background helps one appreciate why some of Klein's papers were formulated in the way they were. Not in respect of her original ideas, but of the need, for example, to clarify disagreements with Fairbairn and to spell out where and how she differed from Freud.

[[RunningHead]]

Asymbolic and Symbolic Play: Developmental Perspectives in the Treatment of Disturbed Children

Monica Lanyado

Monica Lanyado

12 Cluny Avenue
Morningside
Edinburgh EH 10 4RN

Monica Lanyado  

“Put a lot of store on a child's ability to play. If a child is playing, there is room for a symptom or two, and if a child is able to enjoy playing, both alone and with other children, there is no very serious trouble afoot.”

(Winnicott, 1964)

Creativity throughout life relies heavily on the individual's capacity to play with ideas and experiences in the inner world. Innovative work in the Arts and Sciences is often the result of straying from well-established paths and juxtaposing apparently unconnected concepts in a manner which is quite original. For some people this may be a very threatening experience as conforming to the existing book of rules is fundamental to their way of living. Others find these explorations in the inner world exciting, and even fun. “Toying” with ideas confirms and enhances their enjoyment of life, in everyday mundane matters, as well as in their deeper creative experience. This capacity to play in the adult has its roots in childhood and infancy. It is indeed a great gift to be able to play, and without it there is an impoverishment of the quality of relationships to others and relationship to oneself.

Melanie Klein in her development of the psychoanalytic play technique conducted that by providing an analytic setting for the child, such as regularity of session times and constancy of suitable play materials and playroom, the child's free play as well as verbal communication could be used in a similar way to free association in adults. The transference and counter-transference could also be understood through the medium of a child's symbolic play. Inhibition in play was recognised as an important symptom, indicating inhibition in phantasy life and emotional development (Klein, 1955). “The Narrative of a Child Analysis” (Klein, 1961) is a fascinating and detailed example of how she used her understanding of a child's play in her interpretations. Richard was a neurotic child who could express himself symbolically through his play. There are many examples in the Narrative, of anxiety leading to inhibition in play, followed by interpretation freeing play. Dick, an earlier patient of hers (Klein, 1930), alerted Mrs Klein to the difficulties that existed when a child could not adequately symbolise.
